problem: Prior robot-privacy work protects raw or visual sensor data, but structured representations exported to planners, cloud services, logs and learning pipelines (free space, geometry, target references) can still leak household information. Removing explicit fields is often treated as evidence of privacy without measuring residual inference.
motivation: Domestic robots pass derived maps, geometry and target references to downstream components, so raw data staying local is not enough. The authors observe that representations with identical task utility can differ greatly in leakage, and that stronger abstraction does not reliably reduce it. This calls for task-specific, multi-risk evaluation of the complete public export.
key_idea: Task-Functional Perception Distillation (TFPD) keeps rich perception local, exports task-scoped candidate representations, and profiles each by task utility, direct exposure and a vector of residual inference risks measured with representation-aware attackers.
insight: Task equivalence does not imply privacy equivalence: three navigation exports all reach success 1.000 and path ratio 0.898, yet linkability spans 0.532 to 0.970. Abstraction is not monotonic in privacy: topological free space has higher attack point estimates than normalized free space on AI2-THOR, and the order reverses on ProcTHOR. Effects are channel-specific: target region cuts target-category F1 to 0.077, but room and private-object inference stay unchanged across all five object-goal exports. Restricted attackers underestimate leakage: metric-navigation private-object F1 rises from 0.405 to 0.928 with representation-aware features.
method: Task-scoped export construction: for task τ, candidate exports R=D(P) combine directly retained information with a transformed replacement G(π_X(P)) built from locally used information; pure field removal is the special case where nothing is used locally.

Navigation candidates: metric free space, coordinate-normalized free space (removes global origin and scale), and topological node-edge graph (no coordinates or edge lengths); semantics are omitted from all three.
Collision candidates: anonymous exact axis-aligned cuboids versus coarsened cuboids, with centers and sizes rounded to 0.1.
Object-goal candidates: target label (baseline), target coordinate, region, anonymous ID, and planning-graph node; the semantic target is resolved locally and only a functional reference is exported.

Privacy profile Φ=(U,E,L): utility, direct exposure, and a vector of residual inference risks (room, private-object, object-category, target-category, linkability), reported per channel and not collapsed into one score.

Representation-aware attacker protocol: scaled logistic regression, random forest, extra trees and histogram gradient boosting, with feature mappings and model family selected on validation scenes only and then frozen. Baselines are the most-frequent-class predictor and 1/|gallery|. The audit covers 33 representation-attack pairs, 7 already complete and 26 expanded.
Linkability test: 20-scene gallery, queries are perturbed exports (0.30 sparse dropout, 0.10 numeric noise), Top-1 nearest-neighbor retrieval.

setting.backbone: Classical attackers (logistic regression, random forest, extra trees, histogram gradient boosting) trained on exported features; no navigation policy is learned
setting.training_data: Attackers trained on 80 AI2-THOR training scenes (20 validation, 20 test); ProcTHOR replication uses 80/20/20 houses
setting.observation: Simulator ground-truth scene state (free space, object cuboids, target) exported as structured representations; no raw RGB
setting.action_space: Not applicable: privacy evaluation of exports; navigation is A* style planning on the exported free-space graph
setting.simulator: AI2-THOR (120 scenes) plus ProcTHOR-10K (120 houses) and a synthetic diagnostic environment
setting.privileged: Exports are built from simulator ground-truth state; attackers know the schema and transformation but have no hidden semantics

numbers.eval_set_note: 400 held-out episodes; 328 eligible for target category

numbers.extra: Cross-distribution replication; linkability 1.000 metric, 0.573 normalized, 0.497 topological

numbers_note: This is a privacy-evaluation paper with no standard navigation benchmark. Numbers are attack and utility results on the authors' own AI2-THOR and ProcTHOR protocols. Synthetic diagnostics are omitted as non-comparable.
results: Three navigation exports have identical utility (success 1.000, path ratio 0.898) but linkability ranges from 0.532 to 0.970. A target region drops target-category F1 from 1.000 to 0.077 at success 0.995, while coarsening reduces object-category F1 from 0.704 to 0.556 at the cost of collision F1 falling from 1.000 to 0.950. ProcTHOR preserves the inequivalence finding but flips the normalized/topological ordering.
limitations: Simulator-only evaluation; ProcTHOR shares the AI2-THOR engine and there is no real robot
Linkability uses perturbed copies of the same export, not cross-session recapture, and attackers are empirical with no formal guarantee
Representation-aware features are added jointly with no ablation; TFPD only profiles candidates and does not select one at runtime
builds_on: Antonazzi et al. task-specific private representations
